subject: typewriter
pitch: A 1930s typewriter in glossy racing green. Round keys with cream letters on chrome rims in four staggered rows, a semicircle of thin type bars behind them, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller with a sheet of paper half typed, and a small brass maker's badge on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning the three.js module using the agentic-3js-builder SDK, mapping out which API functions like part, joint, chain, and sweep I'll rely on while sticking closely to documented signatures.

Since it's a static prop rather than a creature, I'm deciding to keep the skeleton minimal—just a root joint to attach parts to—and sketching rough dimensions for the typewriter body, keys, and platen so it reads correctly facing forward.

Now I'm laying out specific measurements: a boxy base with small feet, a sloped keyboard deck up front, and the platen/carriage toward the back where paper would feed through.

For keycaps, I'll go simple: cream-colored cylinders for the caps with a thin darker chrome ring beneath for the rim, skipping any letter textures since the svg/texture API is too uncertain to risk—better to keep the geometry clean and manageable.

Each key gets a chrome rim cylinder, dark keytop, and a tiny cream letter glyph, totaling around 105 parts for ~35 keys. For the typebars, I'm arranging thin rotated boxes in a fanning arc behind the keys to suggest the semicircular typebar mechanism.

Simplifying this to a stylized fan of type bars: short box shapes arranged radially along an arc, roughly positioned above the back of the deck so their heads converge toward a central printing point.

Now I'm working out where the platen and paper should sit relative to that arc, placing the roller near the back-top of the machine with the paper sheet wrapping around its front face and extending upward toward the user.

For the paper itself, since textured canvas isn't straightforward, I'll fake typed text with a cluster of tiny dark rectangular boxes arranged in line-like streaks, which should read as typed rows without needing real texture support. Now I'm adding the carriage return lever as a chrome piece near the roller.

Instead of computing a quaternion to orient a cylinder between two points, which the API disallows, I'll use the available helper that directly connects two points with a rod shape, letting me place the lever rod and knob without manual rotation math.

Since the semantics of aim/dir/up are ambiguous, it's safer for me to just bake rotation and translation directly into the geometry itself rather than relying on part's orientation options, then pass a simple centered position.

Writing the box helper function...

I'm also planning a cylinder helper and setting up a flat color palette for the body parts—chrome, racing green, brass, ink—then starting to block out the base body shape dimensions.

Building the body geometry...

Still placing carriage parts...

Now I'm thinking through the typebar arrangement — a semicircular arc of typebars behind the keys, positioned so the hammer heads swing up without colliding with the platen, which means working out the center point, radius, and angular spread carefully.

I'm reconsidering the arc orientation—placing it in the YZ plane puts the fan heads awkwardly behind the keys, so I think it's cleaner to orient the semicircle fan across the XY plane instead, radiating outward toward the printing point from a wider spread of angles.

Positioning the arc near the platen, I'm working out each typebar as a thin radial box rotated around Z so its long axis points outward from the pivot, matching the angle for that key's position in the fan.

For keys, I'm setting up four staggered rows on the sloped panel, computing their positions by mapping local x/z coordinates onto the tilted plane using the panel's rotation angle so each key sits flush on the surface with the correct world-space position and orientation.

I'm working out the math for placing keys on the tilted panel surface, computing how the rotation transforms each key's local offset into world coordinates so they sit flush against the angled top.

Still working out key layout...

With cream letter glyphs made of two small boxes, I'm estimating around 164 parts for keys plus 34 for typebars, well under the triangle budget using low-segment cylinders. For positioning, I'm placing each keycap ring slightly offset along the panel's surface normal from its mounting point so it sits naturally above the sloped panel.

Letter boxes embed slightly into the keytop top surface, which is fine visually. For the chrome rim, I'm considering a flattened torus shape, rotated to lie flush against the keycap surface.

Now I'm figuring out the paper's placement — a thin box geometry near the platen, positioned to emerge and tilt backward naturally like it's feeding out of the typewriter.

Working out the sheet's position more precisely now—centering it near the platen's front edge, tilted back about 0.2 radians, with its bottom resting at the roller top. Then I'm placing small dark boxes as typed text lines stacked across the sheet's visible front face.

Working out the world-space transform for text marks on the tilted sheet, then defining the sheet geometry itself—a thin box rotated by φ and positioned at center C, computing where its bottom edge lands in world coordinates.

I'm adding typed text lines across the lower half of the page, each line made of short word-like rectangles with gaps between them, using a dark ink color. I'm also sketching out the roller/platen as a black cylinder behind the sheet.

Still writing scene geometry...

I'm assuming sweep geometry attaches to the model automatically through the builder, consistent with how other shape helpers work. Now I'm positioning a brass badge on the base's front face, calculating where it falls relative to the angled panel's front edge using the panel's slope coefficients.

Good, badge sits below panel fine. I'm giving the badge a raised brass frame with a dark inner plate, tiny maker lettering, and small brass rivet spheres at the corners. For the body I'm using two shades of racing green -- a base color and a slightly deeper green for the keyboard panel -- plus adding thin chrome trim strips along the base's front and sides.

Now positioning the chrome edge trim and the back raised housing: I'm placing a raised box behind the panel so its front edge meets the panel's back edge cleanly, and checking that the typebar arc sits in front of this housing rather than sinking into it.

I'm working out the typebar fan: rods arranged radially from a pivot point, each a thin box rotated to point outward, with small brass heads at the tips, spanning roughly 17 bars across an 80° arc, colored a dark gunmetal chrome tone, positioned so they clear the platen by a small margin.

Now I'm placing the feet as small black cylinders at the base corners, sizing the base box to sit beneath them, and checking that the tilted panel's geometry stays properly aligned above the base without gaps at the back edge.

Checking the back row at zl -0.07 gives a lower z and higher y, so the keys rise toward the back—matching the typical tilted keyboard profile. That confirms the row spacing works.

Now I'm setting up a helper function to create a bone-attached body joint at the origin, then writing a box helper that bakes geometry parts onto that bone with zero local offset since translation is already applied.

Writing box and cylinder helpers...

For the keyboard panel I'm computing the tilt rotation and translating the box geometry into position before adding it, then working out the math for placing individual keys on the sloped panel surface by rotating the local offset coordinates.

Placing key ring...

Still shaping key glyphs...

Counting up the total parts: keys, typebars, panel pieces, paper and text all add up to roughly 300 components, which seems like a reasonable scene complexity.

Rather than risk uncertainty over the rng API, I'm deciding to sidestep it entirely and use a deterministic hash function based on index (a sine-based pseudo-random formula) so results stay reproducible without depending on an external randomness source.

Now I'm laying out the badge details: a brass box frame with a darker inset plate, cream-colored text bars simulating lettering, and small brass sphere rivets placed at the badge corners, positioning everything relative to the base's front face.

I'm also adding a chrome carriage-return lever with a curved sweep path defined by several waypoints, topped with a black spherical knob and rendered in a cool chrome color.

Now I'm placing the platen knobs as small chrome cylinders rotated to stick out on each side, plus the carriage bar and side brackets as boxes positioned to support the platen roller, checking that their vertical spans overlap sensibly so nothing looks disconnected.

Checking the typebar arc geometry against the platen position confirms clearance, and the paper's vertical range stays consistent. For extra visual flair, I'm considering adding thin chrome or brass pinstripe trim along the panel and base edges to give the typewriter a more polished, detailed look.

Now I'm setting up the key layout math—computing the tilted surface and lift functions for key placement based on the panel's angle, then defining each row of keys with its count, spacing, and stagger offset so the rows feel naturally typewriter-like.

Placing each key's torus ring by lifting it off the surface point and combining the base rotation with the tilt angle to orient it correctly.

Now I'm sizing the keytop cylinder and tilting its axis to match the surface normal, then setting up letter glyphs as randomly chosen bar patterns made of small boxes.

Letter bars will use cream color. Now I'm structuring the builder setup with a body joint, a helper `place` function for positioning parts, and a `boxP` helper for creating box geometry with rotation and color, plus exporting the module's build function and metadata.
